channel.title: ContentMind AI Blog
channel.description: Practical AI, content and growth ideas, daily.

item.title: Give the AI your reader before you give it your topic
item.description: Prompts that start with a topic produce brochure copy. Prompts that start with three sentences about the reader produce a draft that answers the objection they actually have.

item.title: Your AI draft sounds generic because it has never read your work
item.description: The model cannot imitate a voice it has never read. Five of your own posts, pasted before the brief, fix more than any prompt rewrite.

item.title: Your founder story needs a spoken version before a written one
item.description: Most founders polish the written bio and improvise the spoken one. It should be the other way round: the thirty-second answer is the brand.

item.title: The first hour after you post is the whole game
item.description: Most founders publish and walk away. The sixty minutes after a post goes live decide how far it travels and whether a reader ever becomes a client.

item.title: The quarterly content audit: what to retire, refresh, and repeat
item.description: Most founders treat their archive as a museum. Once a quarter, sort every post by the one number that matters — conversations started — and you get a clear retire, refresh, repeat list.

item.title: Use AI to cut the draft, not to write it
item.description: Asking AI for a first draft produces smooth, hollow text. Writing badly yourself and then asking it to cut by forty percent produces your voice, only tighter.

item.title: Your best prompts are worth keeping in one plain text file
item.description: The prompt that finally produced a usable draft is somewhere in your chat history, unfindable. Three headings in a synced text file fix that for good.

item.title: Ghostwritten posts start in a conversation, not a brief
item.description: A brief produces a post about hiring. A recorded conversation produces the story about nearly firing the hire. Only one of them gets read.

item.title: The 200-word ceiling: shorter LinkedIn posts get finished
item.description: Most posts are abandoned at the halfway point. Cutting to 200 words is the cheapest way to earn a read to the end, and the reply that follows.

item.title: Ten evergreen posts beat a hundred forgettable ones
item.description: A hundred posts nobody revisits is a hobby. Ten posts that answer the questions buyers actually ask, kept current, is a content strategy.

item.title: The monthly AI stack audit: keep three tools, cancel the rest
item.description: Most AI subscriptions survive because they are cheap and nobody checks them. A fifteen-minute monthly audit tells you which three tools actually earn their place.

item.title: The redaction habit: using AI on client work without leaking it
item.description: The tasks where AI would save the most time are the ones full of client names and confidential numbers. Redacting the prompt first is what makes them usable.

item.title: Your personal brand compounds only when you repeat yourself
item.description: Founders hunt for new ideas because saying the same thing twice feels lazy. But audiences forget everything except the point you keep coming back to.

item.title: Your LinkedIn headline is a landing page, not a job title
item.description: The line under your name appears on every post, comment and search result you ever show up in. Most founders spend it on a job title nobody asked for.

item.title: Your sales calls are a content calendar you never wrote down
item.description: The questions prospects ask you on calls are the questions your next ten posts should answer. Most founders never write them down.

item.title: Stop asking AI for ideas. Ask it for objections.
item.description: Idea generation is what AI does worst. Turn the request around and ask what a skeptical reader would argue with, and the drafts get sharper fast.

item.title: The three-line brief that fixes most AI drafts
item.description: Better AI drafts come from a better brief, not a better model. Three lines of context do more than any prompt trick.

item.title: The ghostwriter question every founder eventually asks
item.description: Handing over the assembly of a post is not the same as handing over your voice. Here is how to tell the difference before you hire.

item.title: Your comments are doing more for you than your posts
item.description: Most founders spend their LinkedIn energy on publishing. The quieter, higher-return habit is commenting well on a handful of posts each week.

item.title: One idea, seven posts: the founder's content multiplier
item.description: You don't need seven new ideas every week — you need one strong one, cut seven ways. Here is the simple system.

item.title: Why every founder should build in public
item.description: Your customers trust people, not logos. Sharing how you think — wins, doubts and all — is the fastest way to earn that trust.

item.title: The 20-minute LinkedIn post system
item.description: You don't need two hours to write a good post. You need a repeatable loop: one idea, one hook, one edit pass.

item.title: AI won't replace your voice — it will amplify it
item.description: The founders who win with AI aren't the ones who outsource their thinking. They're the ones who use it to think faster.
